title: Generate 3D-printable ornaments in Python: torus knots and golden-angle petals
author: Black
summary: Most 3D-print ornaments are the same snowflake and star. Code can make shapes nobody modeled by hand. Here are two short recipes with manifold3d (Python, pip install manifold3d numpy ). Both output watertight meshes you can slice directly. 1. A torus knot from capsule segments A (p,q) torus knot winds p times around a ring while oscillating q times across the tube. Sample the curve, put a sphere at each point, and union the convex hull of each neighbor pair. That gives a smooth tube with no sweep tool. import math from manifold3d import Manifold import manifold3d as M3 R , r , p , q , t , N = 17 , 5.5 , 3 , 8 , 2.1 , 480 pts = [] for i in range ( N + 1 ): u = 2 * math . pi * i / N rr = R + r * math . cos ( q * u ) pts . append (( rr * math . cos ( p * u ), rr * math . sin ( p * u ), r * math . sin ( q * u ))) sp = [ Manifold . sphere ( t , 14 ). translate ( list ( c )) for c in pts ] segs = [ Manifold . batch_hull ([ sp [ i ], sp [ i + 1 ]]) for i in range ( N )] knot = M3 . Manifold . batch_boolean ( segs , M3 . OpType . Add ) knot = knot . translate ([ 0 , 0 , r + t ]) # lowest point sits on z=0 batch_boolean matters: unioning 480 pieces one by one is far slower. Use a tube radius of at least 1.5x your nozzle width and print it flat with tree supports. 2. Succulent petals from the golden angle Real succulents place each new leaf 137.508 degrees after the last. Scale a sphere into a petal, tilt it, push it outward, and rotate it by i * 137.508 . Small petals start steep in the center and flatten toward the rim. G = math . radians ( 137.508 ) petals = [] for i in range ( 62 ): s = i / 61 L , w , th = 5 + 14 * s , 2.4 + 3.4 * s , 0.9 + 0.5 * s tilt = 78 - 62 * s pt = Manifold . sphere ( 1 , 24 ). scale ([ L , w , th ]) pt = pt . translate ([ L * 0.92 , 0 , 0 ]). rotate ([ 0 , - tilt , 0 ]) pt = pt . translate ([ 1 + 9 * s , 0 , 1.5 + ( 1 - s ) * 7 ]). rotate ([ 0 , 0 , math . degrees ( i * G )]) petals . append ( pt ) rosette = M3 . Manifold . batch_boolean ( petals , M3 . OpType . Add ) rosette = rosette ^ Manifold . cube ([ 200 , 200 , 200 ], True ). translate ([ 0 , 0 , 100 ]) # cut below z=0 The ^ intersection with a big cube keeps only z >= 0 so the model has a flat bed face. Tips that saved me prints Check the render before slicing. A top-down view catches gaps in a knot that a perspective view hides. Hull-of-spheres chains look blobby for organic shapes. For those use Manifold.level_set with a signed distance function. Keep walls at least 2 nozzle widths and bridges short. I turned these into printable ornaments (Celtic knot, succulent rosette, spirograph mandala, Moebius ladder) on Cults3D for $1.27 each if you would rather skip the code. More designs and files on Patreon .

title: One more month of ONS data turned a +23% software trend into -6.3%
author: TheCareery
summary: Last month a post on this account worked through twelve months of UK online job advert volumes for thirteen graduate entry occupations, taken from the ONS dataset "Labour demand volumes by Standard Occupation Classification (SOC 2020), UK". The headline figure was that adverts for programmers and software development professionals were up 23% across the window. The September 2026 edition was released on 23 October 2026. The same calculation, on the same thirteen occupations, from the same table, now reads -6.3%. Nothing was revised. The window moved by one month. What actually changed Programmers and software development professionals, UK total, new online job adverts: Window Start End Change Sep 2025 to Aug 2026 9,404 11,591 +23.3% Oct 2025 to Sep 2026 10,213 9,570 -6.3% August 2026 was a local high. September 2026 came in below the previous October. That is the whole story, and it is worth sitting with, because a twelve month endpoint to endpoint change is a two number statistic and both of those numbers are a single month of adverts. The earlier headline was not wrong about the data. It was over confident about what two months can carry. The fix is not a smarter metric. It is publishing the series and letting people see the shape. The full thirteen, October 2025 to September 2026 Occupation Oct 2025 Sep 2026 Change Sales accounts and business development managers 14,528 14,051 -3.3% IT business analysts, architects and systems designers 7,674 10,205 +33.0% Programmers and software development professionals 10,213 9,570 -6.3% Human resources and industrial relations officers 6,565 7,072 +7.7% Finance and investment analysts and advisers 6,158 5,213 -15.3% Advertising and marketing associate professionals 5,465 5,111 -6.5% Mechanical engineers 2,609 4,842 +85.6% Management consultants and business analysts 3,501 4,633 +32.3% Civil engineers 2,285 2,795 +22.3% Project support officers 1,621 1,691 +4.3% Data analysts 1,606 1,583 -1.4% Chartered and certified accountants 1,582 1,570 -0.8% Graphic and multimedia designers 1,224 1,266 +3.4% Mechanical engineers at +85.6% deserves the same caution as software did. October 2025 was 2,609 and September 2026 was 4,842, but the twelve months in between run from 1,383 to 4,842 and move around a lot. Read the series, not the headline. Two series changes in this edition The July 2026 gap is filled. The August 2026 edition had no July figure for these occupations. The September edition does. Anything published off the August edition that described a July gap is now out of date. March 2026 is suppressed for all thirteen. ONS marks it [x] . A suppression marker is not a zero and should not be treated as one, and it should not be interpolated. Carry it through verbatim or leave the month out. The extraction script Last month this script lived on one machine, which is the opposite of the point of publishing a series. It is now downloadable at thecareery.com/ons-extract.py , and it is boring on purpose: it selects thirteen SOC codes from Table 3, filters to the rows where the region is Total UK , and reshapes wide month columns into long format. It does not adjust, smooth, interpolate or recompute a single figure, and it carries [x] through unchanged. SOC_CODES = [ 2121 , 2122 , 2133 , 2134 , 2142 , 2421 , 2422 , 2431 , 3543 , 3544 , 3554 , 3556 , 3571 ] SHEET = " Table 3 " HEADER_ROW = 5 UK_LABEL = " Total UK " TREND_MONTHS = 12 It has a --verify-against flag that diffs freshly generated CSVs against a published copy and exits non zero on any difference. That is what makes the monthly refresh checkable rather than trusted. The header check is the part that matters most: if str ( header [ 0 ]). strip () != " Region " : sys . exit ( " unexpected header, ONS may have changed the layout, stop and check " ) A silent column shift in a 50 MB workbook is how a pipeline starts publishing confident nonsense. Fail loudly instead. Source and the pages built from it Office for National Statistics, "Labour demand volumes by Standard Occupation Classification (SOC 2020), UK", January 2017 to September 2026 edition, released 23 October 2026, Table 3. Licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. The per occupation breakdowns, including the regional splits and the full twelve month series, are published here: UK job advert volumes by occupation Software developer job adverts Mechanical engineer job adverts Job adverts are not vacancies , the caveat page for anyone tempted to read advert counts as hiring

title: How to Scrape Sainsbury's Grocery Prices with Python
author: ReventaData
summary: By the end of this tutorial, you will have a Python script that pulls grocery prices and promotional offers from Sainsbury's into structured JSON: product name, shelf price in GBP, Nectar card price, promotional text, unit price and unit measure, customer rating, category names, EAN barcodes, and product URL. Sainsbury's is a UK supermarket where shoppers buy groceries online. Tracking grocery prices or checking promotional discounts by hand across dozens of products is tedious, and copying product cards manually into spreadsheets takes hours. In this guide, we use Python and the Apify Actor Sainsbury's Scraper ( reventadata/sainsburys-scraper ). Our benchmark run (configured with searchQueries: ["coffee"] , maxItems: 60 , maxPages: 3 , onlyPromotions: true , exactMatchesOnly: true ) finished in 10.6 seconds and returned 50 products. Time estimate: About 30 minutes. Prerequisites To follow this tutorial, you will need: Python 3.11+ installed locally on your system. The Apify API client for Python ( pip install apify-client ). An Apify account and its API token. Copy your API token from API & Integrations in the Apify Console settings, and then install the official Apify client library in your terminal: pip install apify-client What you'll achieve You will run the Actor from Python and receive clean, structured JSON records for every matching grocery item on Sainsbury's. The scraper reads product records embedded directly in search results, so individual product pages do not need to be opened separately. Note on pricing structures: Sainsbury's displays both standard retail prices and discounted loyalty prices. When a product has a Nectar card discount, price gives that discounted price, priceIsNectar is set to true , and regularPrice stores the standard price before the promotion. Example use case: Suppose you want to track promotional coffee deals across Sainsbury's online catalog. Setting searchQueries: ["coffee"] alongside onlyPromotions: true and exactMatchesOnly: true collects discounted coffee products, up to the maxPages and maxItems caps, with its promotional dates and unit pricing. Step 1: Access Sainsbury's Scraper Open the Sainsbury's Scraper page on Apify Store. The store listing details available input fields, output attributes, and pricing. You can click Try for free to inspect the Actor in the web interface. In this guide, we will invoke the scraper directly using Python code. Step 2: Configure search parameters The primary configuration property is searchQueries , an array of grocery search terms. Each term searches the UK online store at sainsburys.co.uk. Here is a Python script with the same input we used for our benchmark run: from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run_input = { " searchQueries " : [ " coffee " ], " maxItems " : 60 , " maxPages " : 3 , " onlyPromotions " : True , " exactMatchesOnly " : True , " proxyConfiguration " : { " useApifyProxy " : True , " apifyProxyGroups " : [ " UNBLOCKER " ], }, } run = client . actor ( " reventadata/sainsburys-scraper " ). call ( run_input = run_input ) for item in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): print ( item [ " name " ], item [ " price " ], item [ " currency " ], item [ " unitPrice " ], item [ " url " ]) This code uses the exact settings behind the metrics in this article. Setting maxPages: 3 limits pagination to three search result pages, while maxItems: 60 caps saved records across the query. Step 3: Configure optional settings and filters The Actor provides multiple configuration options and filtering switches: Parameter Type Default What it does searchQueries array none List of grocery terms to search on sainsburys.co.uk. maxItems integer 100 Maximum number of products to save across all search queries. maxPages integer 6 Maximum result pages to walk per query (1 to 20, up to 60 products per page). sort string RELEVANCE Sort order: RELEVANCE , PRICE_ASC , PRICE_DESC , or RATING . minPrice , maxPrice number none Price limits in GBP, evaluated after extraction. minRating number none Minimum average customer rating (0 to 5); unrated products are dropped. onlyPromotions boolean false Keeps only items that carry at least one active promotion. exactMatchesOnly boolean false Drops related products appended by search (rows with relevance: 2 ). includeKeywords array none Words the product name or category must contain. excludeKeywords array none Words the product name or category must not contain. proxyConfiguration object Apify Unblocker Proxy settings; Apify Unblocker is required for sainsburys.co.uk requests. Three operational details help you configure these filters effectively: onlyPromotions: true keeps both Nectar discounts and multibuys. Fixed-price promotions report their pre-promotion price in regularPrice . Multibuy deals (such as "Buy any 2 for £7.50 with Nectar") leave regularPrice as null while marking onPromotion: true . exactMatchesOnly: true excludes related search recommendations. The Actor flags exact hits as relevance: 1 and related products as relevance: 2 . Filters run locally on extracted page records. Keyword inclusion, price boundaries, rating thresholds, and promotional checks filter rows before dataset insertion. Step 4: Run the Actor Replace <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> with your actual token, save the file, and execute it. Calling .call() starts the Actor in the Apify cloud and waits for completion. The scraper walks the requested result pages, applies your filtering criteria, and stores saved products into the default dataset. Allow the script to execute until completion. Our benchmark run finished in 10.6 seconds, extracting 50 products across three pages. Each line printed by the script shows the product title, shelf price in GBP, unit price, and product page link. Step 5: View and download results The script loops through items in the dataset using .iterate_items() . In the Apify Console, you can also download dataset records as JSON, CSV, Excel or JSONL. Here is the first product record from our benchmark run ( id: "7620344" ), verbatim: { "id" : "7620344" , "name" : "Nescafé Azera Americano Instant Coffee 90g" , "url" : "https://www.sainsburys.co.uk/groceries/product/nescaf-azera-americano-instant-coffee-90g" , "price" : 3.5 , "currency" : "GBP" , "unitPrice" : 38.89 , "unitMeasure" : "kg" , "regularPrice" : 7.25 , "priceIsNectar" : true , "onPromotion" : true , "promotions" : [ { "type" : "SIMPLE_FIXED_PRICE" , "text" : "Better than Half Price with Nectar" , "isNectar" : true , "regularPrice" : 7.25 , "startsAt" : "2026-10-14T23:00:00Z" , "endsAt" : "2026-11-03T00:00:00Z" } ], "rating" : 4.61 , "reviewCount" : 191 , "categories" : [ "Instant coffee" ], "image" : "https://assets.sainsburys-groceries.co.uk/gol/7620344/image.jpg" , "eans" : [ "7613034065520" , "8445290044822" ], "isAvailable" : true , "relevance" : 1 , "matchedKeyword" : "coffee" , "page" : 1 , "scrapedAt" : "2026-10-23T19:42:19.809562+00:00" } Understanding your results The dataset provides several key pricing and catalog attributes: price : the current shelf price in GBP. When a Nectar price is active, this reflects that loyalty price. regularPrice : the shelf price before a fixed-price promotion, or null for multibuys. unitPrice and unitMeasure : cost per kg or ltr enabling direct comparisons across package sizes. promotions : array with promotion type, text, Nectar requirements, and validity dates. eans : barcode identifiers for matching products against other retailers. Our benchmark run extracted 50 products, yielding clear insights into the coffee category: All 50 products had numeric prices ranging from 1.75 GBP to 16.50 GBP, with a median price of 4.80 GBP. All 50 items were on promotion: 47 had fixed-price Nectar deals with regularPrice populated, and 3 featured multibuy deals (such as "Buy any 2 for £7.50 with Nectar"). 48 products had customer ratings ranging from 3.37 to 5.0 with a median rating of 4.53, backed by 2,897 total reviews across the dataset. 2 products had no customer reviews. All 50 items were exact search matches ( relevance: 1 ), and all 50 items carried EAN barcodes across 15 distinct categories. Pro tips and advanced usage Tune page counts to category volume. Each Sainsbury's search page contains up to 60 products. The default setting of maxPages: 6 checks up to roughly 360 items. For broad categories, increase maxPages up to 20 to capture more results. Standardize price comparisons with unit measures. Rather than comparing raw pack prices, use unitPrice and unitMeasure to evaluate costs per kilogram or per litre across varying brand packaging. Automate alerts with webhooks. You can configure Apify webhooks to trigger downstream HTTP endpoints when a scrape finishes. The payload's resource object contains the run details ( docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/webhooks/actions ), including defaultDatasetId . Cross-reference catalogs using EAN barcodes. The Actor extracts all EAN barcodes into the eans array, allowing reliable product matching against external retail databases. For current pricing and details, see the Store page . Troubleshooting common issues The run fails with "0 rows for queries...". The Actor raises a runtime error when zero rows are pushed to the dataset. This occurs if your search terms yielded no products on the site or if strict filters (such as narrow price boundaries or rating thresholds) rejected every candidate item. The run fails with "searchQueries is empty". You must provide at least one grocery search term in searchQueries . If the list is empty or contains only whitespace, the Actor raises this error before requesting any pages. Input rejected with invalid sort option. The sort parameter accepts only RELEVANCE , PRICE_ASC , PRICE_DESC , or RATING . Any other string is refused before the run starts. For technical support or feature requests, visit the Actor's Store page. Next steps Now that you can extract grocery prices programmatically, you can schedule recurring runs to track supermarket price fluctuations, build inflation trackers, or monitor competitive promotions over time. Explore the Apify Python client documentation and the Store page to learn more. What grocery items are you planning to track on Sainsbury's? Drop a comment below!

title: Building rag-critic: Factual Grounding & Adversarial Hallucination Auditing in LangGraph
author: Shaheer Ul Hassan
summary: When building production Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, the primary failure mode isn't retrieval latency or vector index size— it's silent hallucination . LLMs frequently generate fluent, highly plausible-sounding claims that are completely unsupported by the retrieved reference chunks. In multi-agent systems and mission-critical workflows, accepting an ungrounded draft can corrupt downstream decision-making. To solve this in cyclic multi-agent graphs, I built and published rag-critic on PyPI—a lightweight, adversarial hallucination auditor and citation grounding engine architected specifically for LangGraph . 🔍 The Architectural Bottleneck Standard RAG architectures evaluate answers at a holistic paragraph level using an LLM-as-a-judge. This approach has three major flaws: Coarse-Grained Feedback : Telling an agent "this answer feels inaccurate" doesn't specify which sentence was hallucinated. High Latency : Re-prompting large frontier models for full evaluations adds 3–5 seconds per step. Lack of Determinism : Without an entailment matrix, confidence scores drift across model runs. 📦 Project Links & Open-Source Repositories PyPI Package: pypi.org/project/rag-critic GitHub Repository: github.com/samjanjua6/rag-critic Author Engineering Portfolio: https://shaheerulhassan.com 💻 Quickstart & Python Usage Install directly from PyPI: bash pip install rag-critic from rag_critic import RAGCritic critic = RAGCritic() # Evaluate a draft answer against retrieved source chunks result = critic.evaluate( draft_response="Python was released in 1991 by Guido van Rossum. It was originally named Monty.", retrieved_chunks=[ "Python is an interpreted programming language released in 1991 by Guido van Rossum." ] ) print(f"Status: {result.status}") # REVISE / APPROVED print(f"Grounding Score: {result.grounding_score:.2f}") # e.g. 0.50 print(f"Hallucination Index: {result.hallucination_index:.2f}") # Inspect claim-level verification for claim in result.claims: print(f"[{claim.status.value}] {claim.text}") # [SUPPORTED] Python was released in 1991 by Guido van Rossum. # [UNGROUNDED] It was originally named Monty. from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END from rag_critic import create_critic_node, critic_router builder = StateGraph(MyRAGState) # Add standard generator and retriever nodes builder.add_node("retrieve", retrieve_docs) builder.add_node("generate", generate_draft) # Add rag-critic as an adversarial validation checkpoint builder.add_node("critic", create_critic_node()) builder.add_edge("retrieve", "generate") builder.add_edge("generate", "critic") # Dynamic cyclic routing based on hallucination thresholds builder.add_conditional_edges( "critic", critic_router, { "approved": END, # Output is grounded; return to user "rewrite": "generate", # Minor gaps; instruct re-writer "re_retrieve": "retrieve", # Heavy hallucination; expand search } )

title: 0% of Greenhouse jobs were over 6 months old. That was my bug, not their data
author: Radar Labs
summary: I spent a week assuming my scraper was fine. Then a sanity check told me 0% of Greenhouse postings were older than six months, which is not a thing that happens on a real job board. The culprit was one field. And it is not exotic — if you have ever scraped a job feed, you have probably made the same mistake. The mistake is updated_at Our Greenhouse connector read: postedAt = row . get ( " updated_at " ) or row . get ( " created_at " ) That reads fine. It is wrong twice over. First, the Greenhouse board API does not return created_at for a job, so the fallback never fires. Second — and this is the part that matters — updated_at is when a recruiter last touched the requisition , not when the job went live. Here is what that does to real data. Account Executive, AI Native came back with a recent updated_at . Its actual first_published is 2024-12-20 . A req opened in 2024 and edited yesterday looks one day old. The fix is one line: postedAt = ( row . get ( " first_published " ) or row . get ( " created_at " ) or row . get ( " updated_at " )) first_published exists. It was just not the field we reached for. What it changed Same 259 companies, same day, only the date field changed: with updated_at with first_published median age 22 days 51 days older than 180 days 5.5% 14.2% Greenhouse older than 180 days 0.0% 14.5% The Greenhouse number is the tell. No board has zero stale reqs. 0.0% was not a finding, it was a bug report: the freshness signal had been pinned to "last edited", so every edit reset the clock. If you are filtering scraped jobs by age, or building an "only new since last run" delta on top of posted_at , this bug is silent and total. Every stale req comes back as new, forever. The full age distribution (6,833 postings that publish a salary) Measured 2026-10-24 from each board's own first-published field: p10: 8 days median: 51 days p90: 236 days oldest: 2,628 days (just over seven years) older than 30 days: 65.9% older than 90 days: 30.1% older than 180 days: 14.2% older than a year: 4.9% So the median "open" role has been open for close to two months. Nearly a third are past a quarter, and one in seven is past half a year. Boards differ, and the difference is the date semantics Board Postings Median age p90 Oldest >180d Date field Greenhouse 4,063 52d 236d 2,628d 14.5% first_published Ashby 2,615 46d 215d 1,325d 12.7% createdAt Lever 155 77d 527d 2,230d 30.3% publishedAt Lever postings are older on median and much older in the tail. That is either a different hiring style or a board that keeps reqs visible after the hire — I cannot tell which from the data, so I am not going to dress it up as a conclusion. Companies with the longest-running open reqs (minimum five dated postings): Secureframe median 442 days , Zilliz 430, Character 310, Delfina 299. A stale listing is not proof of a fake job either. Plenty of teams keep a rolling req open for a role they hire into continuously. But if you are a candidate sorting by "newest", a rolling req sorted by updated_at will follow you around forever. The general rule Before you trust any posted_at , answer two questions about it: Which field is it? first_published / createdAt / publishedAt are posting dates. updated_at / modified_at are edit dates. Mixing them is the bug above. Does the board even have the first kind? If it only exposes last-modified, your ages are understated and no amount of downstream maths will fix it — report it separately rather than averaging it in with boards that do it right. A cheap sanity test that would have caught this in minutes: compute the share of postings older than six months, per board. If any real board comes back at 0%, you are not measuring what you think you are measuring. The age numbers and the per-company breakdown live at radarlabs.surge.sh/freshness.html , regenerated weekly from the companies' own public feeds. The underlying postings, with dates and salary ranges, are a free CC BY 4.0 CSV — 6,833 rows across 259 companies. If you would rather not run the scraping yourself, the same data is available as a paid Apify Actor, and I would rather you read the free CSV first and decide whether it is worth $0.0015 a row.

title: 84% of abandoned v0 apps run a known-exploited Next.js
author: MacroCyber
summary: A field note on what happens to AI-built apps after the builder walks away, measured on October 21, 2026, the day Next.js 15 left security support. Of 274 abandoned v0-built apps whose Next.js version we could read, 231 (84%) declare a version inside the React2Shell range, the remote code execution flaw CISA has listed as actively exploited since December 5, 2025. 226 of them run the exact same version: Next.js 15.2.4 . Only 3 run Next.js 16, and none runs the current patched release. The date matters for a second reason. Next.js 15 was released on October 21, 2024, and the Next.js support policy keeps a major in Maintenance LTS for two years. Since October 21, 2026, the policy sends security fixes to Next.js 16 only . That leaves 271 of the 274 apps on a major outside its support window , on top of the 231 already in a known-exploited range. This note explains how we measured it, why so many apps landed on one version, what the numbers do and do not prove, and what to do if one of these apps is yours. 1. What we measured We wanted apps that were generated by an AI builder, deployed, and then left alone. v0 makes that population easy to find without guessing: projects it syncs to GitHub carry a recognizable notice in their README. We searched public GitHub repositories with that notice, created between January and August 2025 , whose last push was before October 1, 2025 , and that list a live homepage. That gave 398 apps , each untouched for more than a year. For each one we fetched the homepage and the JavaScript files it links, exactly what any visitor's browser downloads. An App Router build of Next.js declares its own version in that code (a line of the form window.next = { version: "15.2.4", appDir: true } ), and that self-reported version is what we recorded. We sent no exploit, no crafted request and no login attempt , and we are not publishing any app's address. Result Apps Sampled (v0 notice, created Jan to Aug 2025, no push since Sep 30, 2025) 398 Still serving a page 304 Next.js version readable from the served code 274 Version inside the React2Shell range (CVE-2025-55182, on CISA KEV) 231 On Next.js 14, out of support since October 2025 39 On Next.js 15, out of support since October 21, 2026, already patched for React2Shell 1 On Next.js 16, the only supported major 3 On the current patched release (16.4.2) 0 The other 94 apps were gone or unreadable: 69 answered 404 (a deleted deployment), 7 answered 402 (a paused Vercel project), and the rest timed out, no longer resolved, or ran a build whose version we could not read. 2. Why one version dominates: the exact pin The concentration on 15.2.4 is not a coincidence, and it is not about people choosing an old version. We opened the package.json of sampled repositories, and the generated projects of that period declare "next": "15.2.4" with no range operator . An exact pin means a fresh install, a rebuild or a redeploy all produce the same 15.2.4 forever. Nothing upstream can move the app forward. Only a person editing that line can. That turns a normal software habit into a trap. In a hand-maintained project, an exact pin is a deliberate choice somebody revisits. In a generated project, it is a snapshot of the day the model wrote the file , and the builder who accepted it usually never opened package.json at all. The 35 apps on 14.2.16 show the same pattern from an earlier template: one version, pinned, frozen. Then the builder moved on. Every app in this sample was created in a burst of experimentation in 2025 and has not received a single commit in over a year. The deployment kept running anyway, because hosting a small app costs nothing and nobody turns it off. The app outlived the attention of the person who made it , and the version it was generated with became its permanent version. 3. What React2Shell is, and what the numbers do not prove CVE-2025-55182 , known as React2Shell, is unauthenticated remote code execution in React Server Components , which the Next.js App Router uses. It affects every Next.js 15 release line and 16.0 until that line's patch (15.2.6 for the 15.2 line), and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on December 5, 2025. Its one precondition, the App Router, is stated on the same line as the version we read, which is why a version in range is a meaningful signal and not a guess. It is still not proof that any of these apps can be compromised today , and we want to be precise about why: Most of these apps sit behind Vercel's firewall. 266 of the 274 are hosted on vercel.app , where Vercel deployed firewall rules against React2Shell for every project. Vercel itself says those rules cannot guarantee protection against all possible variants of an attack and that upgrading is the fix, and researchers have found ways around some WAF defenses . A firewall rule is a mitigation in front of vulnerable code, not a patch to it. The version is self-reported. It is what the served code declares, which is the version that was built. We did not test whether the flaw can be triggered, and we will not. The sample is v0 projects on public GitHub. Builders who kept their repositories private, or who used other tools, are not in it. We think the mechanism (exact pins plus abandonment) generalizes, but the 84% figure describes this population. What the numbers do show is the gap between how long an AI-built app keeps running and how long anyone maintains it . The fix for React2Shell has existed for more than ten months, and 84% of this population never received it. 4. The second problem started on October 21 Even the apps outside the exploited range are not in a safe place. Next.js 14 left its support window in October 2025, and 37 of the 39 apps on it run a version below the fix for the March 2025 middleware authorization bypass , which matters for any app that checks sign-in in middleware. Since October 21, 2026, Next.js 15 joins it. The October 14 security release , two critical fixes and one high, was the last that 15.x was owed under the support policy. Vercel has made exceptions for severe flaws before (it shipped 14.2.35 in December 2025, after 14 had left support), but an exception only helps an app that installs it. A pinned, abandoned app misses every patch equally : the ones that ship for its line and the ones that never will. 5. If one of these apps is yours The cheapest fix is often the right one. An app you no longer use should not be running. Delete the deployment or pause the project, and the exposure is gone along with everything else it might hold (an API key in its code, a database it still talks to). For an app you want to keep: Upgrade Next.js to 16. The official upgrade guide covers the breaking changes, and a codemod handles most of them. A generated app is usually small enough that this takes minutes, not days. Replace the exact pin with a range ( "next": "^16.4.2" ), so a rebuild picks up patch releases. Turn on automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) in the repository, so the next advisory arrives as a pull request instead of as nothing. Check what the live app actually serves , not what you remember deploying. MacroCyber reads the Next.js version an App Router site serves and flags it when it falls inside a range CISA lists as exploited, as a signal to verify, alongside the AI-era exposures it was built for (open Supabase and Firebase databases, leaked AI keys, exposed MCP servers). You can scan any site free , or give your coding agent the same check with our MCP server so it can scan what it just deployed and confirm its own fix. If your app runs on Supabase, the Supabase exposure check covers the other common way abandoned AI-built apps leak. 6. Method details Population: public GitHub repositories whose README carries v0's sync notice, found through GitHub's repository search, one query per creation month from January to August 2025, restricted to repositories last pushed before October 1, 2025 and listing a homepage. Four repositories that had been pushed after that date by the time we read them were excluded. Reading: one GET of the homepage and of the Next.js JavaScript files it references, with a user agent naming MacroCyber, on October 21, 2026. The version is the one the App Router runtime declares in the served code. Matching: versions were matched with the same advisory table the MacroCyber scanner uses, so the article and the product cannot disagree. Publication: aggregate figures only. No app is named. This note reflects data read on October 21, 2026. Versions, hosting protections and support dates change, so check the current Next.js advisories before acting on any single figure. Originally published on macrocyber.co . Written with AI assistance from data we collected on October 21, 2026, and checked against it.

title: I built 1,500+ browser tools that never upload your files
author: Joseph Orduna
summary: The site is Practical Web Tools . It has 1,500+ free tools: file converters, PDF tools, a couple hundred calculators, some dev utilities, and twelve creative apps. The one thing they all share is that your files never leave your device. There is no upload step, because there is no server doing the work. It started much smaller, a few dozen converters, and it grew for a reason that surprised me: client-side meant every new tool cost me nothing to run. I want to walk through how the thing actually works, because "it runs in your browser" gets hand-waved a lot. From file to WebAssembly Every tool starts the same way. You pick a file, the page gets a File object through the File API, and the bytes go into WebAssembly. What happens next depends on the tool: Audio and video run through ffmpeg.wasm, which is ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. MP4 to MP3, audio extraction, format reshuffling: the same ffmpeg you'd call from a terminal, running in a tab. PDF operations use qpdf.wasm. Merging PDFs means concatenating page trees in wasm and handing you back a Blob to download. Splitting and compressing work the same way, with the file's bytes never crossing the network. Images are mostly the canvas API. The HEIC to JPG converter decodes the HEIC in wasm, draws the decoded image to a canvas, and re-encodes it as JPEG at whatever quality you picked. That last category is the one I like demoing, because the privacy claim is checkable by the person using it. Open the dev tools network tab, convert a photo, and watch: no POST with your file, ever. Nothing to take my word for, which beats reading a privacy policy. One wrinkle worth knowing if you go this route: the heavy wasm binaries are lazy-loaded per tool, so someone landing on a converter only downloads the module that converter needs. The HEIC decoder doesn't ship to the mortgage calculator page. Boring discipline, but it's the difference between a fast site and a 40MB homepage. How 1,500+ tools stay maintainable The count is only possible because most tools share plumbing. Converters run through one master template wired to a tool registry, so a new format pair is mostly data (accepted inputs, output format, which wasm module handles it) rather than a new page to build by hand. That's also an honest caveat about the number, which I'll get to. The heavier piece is threading. Some of the creative apps want multithreaded wasm, which needs SharedArrayBuffer , which means serving COOP and COEP headers on those routes so the browser treats the page as cross-origin isolated. Those headers have knock-on effects for embedding third-party scripts, so the isolation is scoped to the routes that actually need it. Small detail, real hours. The Studio end of the pool The converters are table stakes. The part people don't expect is the Studio : twelve free creative apps, all client-side. A photo editor with layers and masks, a vector editor, a multitrack video editor (yes, ffmpeg.wasm again), an audio DAW, motion graphics, page layout, a PDF organizer, a RAW photo library — plus Blender, FreeCAD, a 3D-print slicer, and GNU Octave running in the tab. None of them are Photoshop. All of them open in two clicks with no account and no install, which turns out to be the actual feature people want. Why client-side beats a server here Two reasons, one principled and one embarrassingly practical. The principled one: people convert private things. Contracts, tax documents, ID scans, photos they'd rather not explain. A server-side converter asks you to trust its retention policy, its cloud provider, and its future acquirers. A client-side converter doesn't have anything to retain. I couldn't leak your file if I wanted to, because I never receive it. The practical one: compute is what kills sites like this. A server-side converter needs upload handling, storage, a conversion queue, temp-file cleanup jobs, and egress bandwidth, all sized for peak load. My version needs static hosting and a CDN. The 1,400th tool costs me the same as the first one, which is roughly nothing. That is the only reason a solo dev can run 1,500+ tools on ad revenue. It's also an installable PWA. Tools you've opened keep working offline, since the code is already on your machine. Honest limitations Every "free and private" pitch deserves this list: Ads pay for it. They're on the site. That's the whole business model, no mystery. Some tools are thin. The 460+ unit converters are a formula with a UI wrapped around them, and the tool count is big partly because format pairs multiply: every input format times every output format. Fluffing the count was never the goal, but the count does flatter the site. A browser tab is not a native app. WebAssembly is slower than native code and browsers cap tab memory. A desktop ffmpeg install beats the browser on large files every time. If you convert video daily, use a native tool. This site is for the person who needs it once and doesn't want to install anything. The first conversion has a wait. The heavy wasm binaries are several megabytes and only load when you open a tool that needs one. Quality varies. Exotic codecs and badly-built PDFs don't always survive conversion. It's real ffmpeg and real qpdf, but with real browser constraints around them. What I'd like feedback on If you try it: does a specific tool misbehave in your browser, Safari quirks especially? Which converter is too limited for your actual workflow? And is there a task where "in the browser" genuinely doesn't cut it? That list is basically my roadmap. The site is here .

title: Why a "$75/hr" freelance rate is often $34/hr net (so I built a free client-side calculator to fix it)
author: kovrastudio
summary: One of the most expensive mistakes independent developers, designers, and solo consultants make is pricing projects using "salary math" ( $100,000 / 2,000 hours = $50/hr ). In reality, three silent leaks eat freelance margins alive: Billable Utilization (~55–65%): Between scoping, debugging client environments, proposals, admin, and context switching, most solo operators only bill 22–25 hours out of a 40-hour desk week. Self-Employment Taxes & Overhead: Setting aside 25–30% for taxes plus annual SaaS/hardware burn cuts raw hourly numbers dramatically. Reverse Payment Fees & Uncapped Revisions: Charging $2,500 via international PayPal, Stripe FX, or Upwork doesn't net $2,500 — unless you calculate the reverse gross invoice ( (Net + Fixed Fee) / (1 - % Fee) ). And two "quick weekend tweaks" without a revision cap quietly drop your effective hourly rate by 30%. So I built RateShield (100% Free, Static, Zero Signup) I wanted a fast single-page bookmark I could open before quoting any sprint or client milestone, without logins, cookies, or email walls. Live tool: https://kovrastudio.github.io/ It runs entirely client-side in vanilla HTML/CSS/JS and includes three utilities: 01. True Rate & Sprint Calculator: Plug in your target net take-home pay, tax reserve %, overhead, weeks off, and realistic billable % to see your Minimum Safe Hourly Floor , 8h Day Rate , Weekly Sprint Rate , and Fixed-Project Anchor . 02. Reverse Platform Fee Table: Enter the exact net payout you want to keep and copy the exact invoice amount for Stripe (Domestic & International), PayPal, Upwork, Gumroad, and Fiverr. 03. Pre-Kickoff Scope Creep Risk Scorer: A quick 6-point SOW checklist that estimates potential unpaid margin leak before you send a contract, plus a sample revision-cap clause. (For anyone who also wants a full multi-tab Excel/Google Sheets CFO tracker, editable independent contractor agreement + paid change-order form, and client negotiation scripts, I also linked our complete Solo Operator Kit inside the page — though the web calculator itself is 100% free forever). Would love feedback from fellow freelancers and indie devs: what other payment processors or pricing models (retainers, value-based tiers) would you find useful in v2?

title: Prilizer: stop rereading every pull request
author: Huzaifa Rehman
summary: My entry for Hacktoberfest Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built A reviewer asks for a test. You read the message, push another commit, and come back later. The thread has moved on. Was the request satisfied, withdrawn, or simply buried? Prilizer is a local catch-up desk for up to three public pull requests by one contributor. It reads PR bodies, comments, reviews and inline comments, then uses a local Qwen3 model to identify requests and explain changed discussion. Each action carries the original quote and a GitHub link. The piece I care about most is what happens on the next refresh. An outstanding request stays visible even if the next summary omits it. Marking a digest reviewed only records that you read it. A request leaves the active list after explicit source confirmation, a local dismissal, or a fresh closed/merged state. Closing a PR does not prove the requested code was fixed. If collection is partial or the model fails, the card says Check manually and keeps the older evidence. The app never posts a reply or resolves a GitHub thread. Demo Source and setup · Watch the uncut walkthrough This is the actual app with fictional discussion and simulated GitHub/model responses. The uncut walkthrough shows review, local dismissal, edited evidence and a partial-fetch failure. It is fixture playback, not a live model or customer session. Code Prilizer on GitHub . The repository includes setup, evaluation inputs, raw outputs and failed runs. How I Built It A React page talks to a loopback Node server. A bounded anonymous collector keeps discussion channels separate and compares complete snapshots. Qwen3 1.7B proposes structured requests; application code validates quotes and provenance, then persists requests independently of the next model summary. The intended shortcut is opening one small desk instead of reconstructing several conversations. Refresh is manual, unchanged successful analysis is cached, and older requests remain visible. There is no notification feed to keep watching. I have not measured how much human review time this saves. I would rather leave that question open than turn a fast cache read into a claim about someone's working day. What Worked, and What Didn't The first frozen evaluation failed: 8/12 correct outcomes, including one false Waiting. The model missed indirect requests and confused who was asking whom. I added source-role and fresh-confirmation constraints, retained the failures, and froze twelve different synthetic cases before the next run. The revised pipeline scored 12/12 , with zero false Waiting results and zero invalid action quotes. A fixed keyword baseline scored 10/12 , with one false Waiting. The model picked up an approval condition that the keyword baseline missed. That result belongs to the full pipeline, including deterministic persistence and validation. It does not establish general reliability. Summary wording was not scored; manual inspection still found misleading actor attribution in two summaries. Speed is another limit. Fresh-set model calls took 8.4–47.1 seconds. A real Docker CLI PR took 47.3 seconds, then reused its analysis on an unchanged refresh. A Node.js PR hit the 60-second timeout twice. The app kept it at Check manually. My 30-second target remains unmet. Raw results and the earlier failures are retained . Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Qwen3's open weights and Ollama let the interpretation run on the same laptop as the saved discussion. GitHub still needs a network connection for fresh data; cached evidence remains readable offline. The model proposes meaning; inspectable application code checks source IDs, exact quotes, actor eligibility, freshness and request persistence. I can change those rules or test another local model without depending on a hosted inference endpoint. There is no per-request inference API bill. Hardware, electricity, memory and waiting still cost something. The open approach makes this local workflow possible, while the measurements show where it is still too slow.

title: When a student misspells a word, does a small AI model quote it back exactly less often? A preregistered test came back underpowered
author: munimv2
summary: This work was made with AI agents working in my name. I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The study was preregistered before any data was collected, the code is open (Apache-2.0), and the write-up below reports the outcome whatever it turned out to be. It turned out to be an honest "we could not decide yet," and that is worth writing down too. The question When a small AI model gives feedback on a student's essay and quotes the student's own words back to them, how faithfully does it copy those words? And does it copy them less faithfully when the quoted passage contains a misspelling? That matters for formative writing feedback. If a tool silently "tidies up" a learner's misspelled phrase when it quotes them, the student loses the chance to see and fix their own error, and the feedback is quietly misreporting what they wrote. Where this came from This is the third preregistered study in a line I have been running on quote fidelity in AI writing feedback, all on the public ELLIPSE corpus of English-language-learner essays (Crossley et al., 2023), using two small local models, llama3.2:3b and qwen2.5:3b, each writing feedback in English and in Spanish. Study v2 and study v3 both found that these models usually quote learners verbatim: about nine times in ten. v3's preregistered band test found no clear overall difference, but one of its post hoc (not preregistered) contrasts stood out — for the qwen2.5:3b Spanish cell, quotes over a passage containing a misspelling were reproduced exactly less often than quotes over a clean passage, with a 95% interval that excluded zero. v3 called that "a lead for a future preregistered study, not a finding." v4 is that study: a confirmatory, passage-level test on a fresh, non-overlapping essay sample. The preregistered rule, fixed before any data H1 (directional): on fresh essays, a quote is reproduced exactly less often when the student passage behind it contains a misspelling than when it is clean. The primary outcome was the exact-quote rate on misspelled passages minus the rate on clean passages, pooled over the four model-by-language cells, with each essay's quotes kept together and a 95% interval from 10,000 whole-essay bootstrap resamples. I also wrote down a power floor in advance: at least 150 quotes of each passage kind, and below that floor the test is reported as underpowered and the sign of the gap is not interpreted. That last clause is the one that ends up mattering. What happened The analysis ran in a sealed container on 2026-10-23, pinned to a fixed research commit, with offline unit tests and a byte-for-byte copy check passing before any numbers were read. Of the 120 preregistered essays, 29 were completed in all four cells (an essay only counts if every cell returned a usable reply for it). Those 29 essays produced 453 matched quotes: 122 over a passage with at least one misspelled word, and 331 over a clean passage. Primary outcome, pooled over all four cells: misspelled passages were quoted exactly 110 of 122 times (90.2%), clean passages 314 of 331 times (94.9%), a gap of -0.047 with a 95% bootstrap interval of -0.125 to +0.036 . The honest verdict: underpowered Only 122 misspelled-passage quotes landed, below the preregistered floor of 150. So by the rule I wrote down in advance, the result is reported as underpowered and its direction is not read as evidence. The interval spans zero in any case. For the record, the point estimate and three of the four per-cell estimates lean in H1's direction, and the qwen2.5:3b English cell leans hardest (gap -0.150, interval -0.346 to +0.036). But the study was not built to carry that weight, so I claim nothing from it. Notably, this does not replicate v3's qwen Spanish lead, which here sat at +0.008 — consistent with that lead being specific to one cell and language rather than a general effect. Why it came up short, and what a conclusive v5 needs The binding constraint was quote count, not essay count. v4 kept v3's per-cell time budget, but the analysis set is the intersection of four cells run on CPU, and the slowest cell (qwen2.5:3b in English, about 147 seconds per request) reached only part of the sample. The intersection of four partly-completed cells, minus failed requests, left 29 essays and 122 misspelled-passage quotes. A powered v5 should budget from v4's measured seconds per request so every cell reaches all 120 essays — roughly twice the request budget or double the CPU for the slowest cell, and matching cell speeds to shrink the four-cell intersection cost — lifting the misspelled-passage count above the floor. That is the clean path to actually decide H1. Why I think this is new, and its limits Best-effort prior-art search (VerbatimEval, E-Bench, PEARL, and faithfulness work on LLM writing feedback) turned up tools that measure verbatim reproduction or faithfulness in other settings, but none that tests whether a student passage's misspelling changes how verbatim an AI feedback quote is, split by writing-conventions band. "Found none" is not "none exists," but this is a genuine first attempt at that specific question. Limits, stated plainly: two 3B models, one prompt, one request seed, two feedback languages, one corpus, and a small completed sample. The spell check uses an English dictionary, so real-word errors (their/there) are not detected, and an edge-trimming step can drop a corrected word from the matched passage — which makes a gap harder to find, not easier. No essay text is published; ELLIPSE is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and this is non-commercial research. The takeaway An underpowered result is still a result. Across three preregistered studies the stable finding holds — these small models usually quote English learners verbatim, about nine times in ten — and no study of mine has yet shown that weaker passages are quoted less faithfully. v4 did not have the data to decide, it does not replicate v3's post hoc lead, and it sizes exactly what a powered v5 would need. The full write-up, preregistration, analysis outputs and code are in the open: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/feedback-commons/blob/main/research/RESULTS-v4.md Made with AI agents working in my name. — MV2, Munim, Inc.

title: Hooks de Claude Code: qué son y 3 ejemplos para copiar
author: El Telar
summary: Un hook es un comando que Claude Code ejecuta automáticamente en un momento concreto : después de editar un archivo, antes de ejecutar una orden o cuando te espera. Según la documentación oficial, dan un control determinista: la acción ocurre siempre, sin depender de que el modelo se acuerde. 1. Notificación cuando Claude te espera (macOS) En ~/.claude/settings.json : { "hooks" : { "Notification" : [ { "matcher" : "" , "hooks" : [ { "type" : "command" , "command" : "osascript -e 'display notification \" Claude Code needs your attention \" with title \" Claude Code \" '" } ] } ] } } Escribe /hooks para comprobar que aparece. Si no suena, activa las notificaciones de Script Editor en Ajustes del Sistema. 2. Prettier tras cada edición { "hooks" : { "PostToolUse" : [ { "matcher" : "Edit|Write" , "hooks" : [{ "type" : "command" , "command" : "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" }] } ] } } 3. Bloquear archivos protegidos Un script que termina con código 2 bloquea la acción y Claude recibe el mensaje: #!/bin/bash INPUT = $( cat ) FILE_PATH = $( echo " $INPUT " | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' ) for pattern in ".env" "package-lock.json" ".git/" ; do if [[ " $FILE_PATH " == * " $pattern " * ]] ; then echo "Blocked: $FILE_PATH matches ' $pattern '" > &2 exit 2 fi done exit 0 Regístralo como hook PreToolUse con matcher: "Edit|Write" . Guía completa, con diagrama, dónde se guardan y preguntas frecuentes: eltelar.es .

title: AI product UX beyond the chat box
author: Ayraix
summary: The pattern: Shipping "ChatGPT but for our domain" is the fastest way to a confusing product. Users already have a chat app. What they need is AI that shows up inside the job — draft, suggest, transform, explain — with an undo button and a clear owner. Why it matters: Chat interfaces hide structure. They bury status, make errors conversational, and train users to restate context the app already has. Better AI UX treats the model as a coworker with a ticket, not a mystical oracle in a sidebar. Patterns that beat the empty text field Embedded actions — "Summarize this invoice," "Propose settle plan," "Explain this ABAP dump" on the object itself. Reviewable drafts — AI writes; humans approve. Diff views beat streaming monologues. Progressive disclosure — start with a safe suggestion; reveal deeper tools after trust is earned. State you can see — sources used, confidence, and next step — not just a green checkmark. Enterprise angle (without the buzzwords) In ERP and ops tools, the winning UX is often a structured form with an AI assist lane — not a free-form agent that can click anything. Permissioned actions plus audit logs beat open-ended autonomy for most business workflows. What we'd watch next Design systems that treat AI affordances as first-class components (draft chip, cite popover, approve/reject) instead of bolting a chat widget onto every screen. Originally published on ayraix.com , practical AI for enterprise builders.

title: What a Production Brief Should Say When the Data Is Incomplete
author: Ricardo Feldhaus Krisanoski
summary: A production brief can be well written and still give the team the wrong impression of readiness. The danger is especially clear when the report combines current facts with missing channel data or unresolved dependencies. In my public operating-layer case, the daily brief connects normalized demand with deadlines, stages, artwork, materials, approvals and exceptions. Human prioritization remains part of the flow. This technical note develops how the brief should communicate incomplete information. It does not introduce a new deployment or claim a measured planning improvement. Completeness has more than one meaning An order can be present in the operational layer while its artwork approval remains unknown. A source can be reachable while its latest update is unavailable. A report can contain every field it was programmed to display while excluding a channel whose ingestion failed. Those are different gaps. A single “complete” indicator would make them difficult to distinguish. For a report design, I would separate source coverage, record readiness and decision readiness. Source coverage describes which inputs contributed. Record readiness describes the dependencies known for a particular item. Decision readiness describes whether the person has enough evidence and authority to select the next action. These are proposed reporting distinctions. The public case establishes the need to disclose missing coverage and uncertainty; it does not certify this exact field structure. An invented morning brief Consider a fictional brief with two visible work items. One has a confirmed deadline and material availability but still needs artwork approval. The other has an approved design, while its delivery commitment could not be refreshed from the source. Suppose another sales channel did not contribute data to this run. A polished summary saying “today's work is ready” would hide both item-level and coverage-level uncertainty. A more useful brief would state the known dependencies, identify the stale commitment, disclose the excluded channel and direct the unresolved decisions to a person. It would not invent an approval, silently reuse a date as current or claim that the visible items represent all demand. This is an invented example, not a real order list or a report from a production team. Facts should remain separate from interpretation The operating-layer case calculates and reconciles facts before AI interpretation. That separation helps when the report is incomplete. The fact layer can state what arrived, what was checked and what remains unknown. The narrative can explain why an exception deserves attention. The explanation should not transform uncertainty into a confident priority simply to produce a cleaner opening paragraph. I would also preserve the source relationship behind important statements. If the brief says that approval is missing, a reviewer should be able to determine whether the source explicitly says “pending” or whether the approval source was unavailable. The operating responses can be very different. A generation timestamp alone cannot settle that question. The report may be newly generated from older or partially missing inputs. Freshness belongs to the contributing facts as well as the final document. A checklist for a partial brief Does the opening state which sources contributed and which did not? Are unknown, pending and conflicting dependencies distinguishable? Can the reader identify stale facts without inspecting every system? Are statements about “all work” supported by actual source coverage? Does each exception show the decision or clarification still required? Can a person correct or reprioritize the brief without losing the original context? Are report generation and delivery retries kept from duplicating operational work? The purpose is a usable partial report, not a perfect-looking report. Whether it helps the team would need evidence such as corrections, missed dependencies and planning effort measured against an appropriate baseline. The public operating-layer case describes the brief's role in the larger system and keeps quantitative benefits as metrics to collect. If an input disappears tomorrow morning, will your production brief explain the missing coverage before anyone acts on its priorities?
